metadata.title: Measured, Not Taught.
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Hindi. Wagwan is Bear's only — Liam never takes it (IN-FOR-BEAR LAW).
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity skin throughout. UI beats at B00 / B05 ask / verdict / handoff / outro only (ILLUSTRATE LAW); every body beat is a purpose-built C3 concept illustration on the cream stage with exactly one terracotta moment.
metadata.note: Project-update reel for the TaskBoard recovery environment. EVERY number on screen is measured and traceable to recovery-env/REPORT.md and results/*.json — scripted ladder (200 seeds), SFT val loss, SFT success (50 seeds). Nothing illustrative, nothing rounded in the agent's favour. The reel's claim is deliberately a negative result: the environment discriminates recovery, the training did not learn it, and the no-fault control split is what distinguishes the two.

beats.narration: Hi, I am Rohan, and this video is about an RL environment I built to teach an agent to recover when an API call fails. The voice you're hearing is AI narration of my work. The environment measures recovery beautifully. It taught the model nothing at all, and the check that would have told me so in about a minute is the one I skipped.

props.command: Build me an RL environment from a stateful ticket API that trains one capability: recovering from failed calls. Verifiable reward, injected faults, held-out evaluation. Then tell me honestly whether training on it actually improves recovery.

beats.narration: Here's the frame before any detail. When a training run shows no learning, the instinct is to blame the environment you built. Sometimes the model simply cannot do the task yet. One cheap control split tells you which one you're looking at.

beats.narration: The environment is a ticket API. A goal in plain English, the agent emits one JSON call at a time, the service mutates or it fails. Reward is binary and it lands once, at the end: does the final state match what the goal asked for. Not the path. Just the state.

API card arrives, arrows connect the three
terracotta reward check slides up beneath the row

beats.narration: This pair is the whole design. Two timeouts. Byte for byte the same error. On the left the call never landed, so retrying is right. On the right it landed and then timed out, so retrying quietly creates a duplicate. You cannot pattern-match your way out of that. You have to go and look.

left caption types under its card
right caption types under its card
the two columns drift apart; verdicts resolve, the duplicate in terracotta

beats.narration: So does the environment actually see recovery? Three scripted policies, identical planners, differing only in how they handle a failure.

props.command: Run the three scripted policies over 200 eval seeds on the held-out fault types, and chart success rate by policy.

beats.narration_text: So does the environment actually see recovery? Three scripted policies, identical planners, differing only in how they handle a failure.

beats.narration: On fault types it never saw in training: blind retry gets forty-one percent. Re-reading state after an error buys eleven points. Verifying before you finish takes it to one hundred. Same planner, same tasks — the only variable is recovery, and the environment resolves it cleanly.

show.event: second bar grows to 0.41, counter ticks up with it
third bar grows to 0.52
fourth bar grows full width in terracotta, counter lands on 1.00
spark line sets at the foot of the frame

beats.narration_text: On fault types it never saw in training: blind retry gets forty-one percent. Re-reading state after an error buys eleven points. Verifying before you finish takes it to one hundred. Same planner, same tasks — the only variable is recovery, and the environment resolves it cleanly.

beats.narration: Then I trained on it. Supervised fine-tuning on scripted demonstrations, five hundred iterations. Validation loss falls from one point eight eight to nought point one three five — textbook. Task success never leaves the floor. The model learned the shape of a tool call and hallucinated the ticket IDs inside it.

beats.narration: Here's the split that makes it readable. Same three models, no faults injected at all. Four percent, zero, sixteen percent — on tasks where nothing goes wrong. The scripted policy scores one hundred on that same split. So this isn't a failure to recover. The model can't do the task yet.

props.sparkLine: A floor, not a failure to recover.

beats.narration_text: Here's the split that makes it readable. Same three models, no faults injected at all. Four percent, zero, sixteen percent — on tasks where nothing goes wrong. The scripted policy scores one hundred on that same split. So this isn't a failure to recover. The model can't do the task yet.

beats.narration: So the verdict splits. The environment is real: tested, exploit-audited, and it separates recovery across two hundred seeds. The capability claim is not proven — it's unproven, which is not the same as refuted. And I never ran the reinforcement learning stage, because with success at zero every rollout group scores the same and the gradient is zero too.

beats.narration: Your turn, and this one is worth running before you train anything. Paste this into Claude: take the hardest task in your own repo, and ask it for the cheapest check that would tell you your model can't do the task at all — separately from whether it can't recover. Look for whether the check it proposes runs in under a minute. If it's expensive, it's the wrong check, and you'll skip it exactly like I did.

props.command: Take the hardest multi-step task in my repo. Design the cheapest possible control condition that separates "the model cannot do this task at all" from "the model cannot recover when it fails" — and tell me what result would make me stop and rebuild rather than train.
